title: Mobile SEO Platforms: What to Look for in Tools and Software

meta_description: What to look for in a mobile SEO platform: smartphone crawling, real-user Core Web Vitals with INP, mobile rank tracking, and clean reporting.
excerpt: No single tool covers all of mobile SEO. Here's what a mobile SEO platform should do and how to choose tools that fit your site and team.

topic: Buyer's guide to the features that matter in mobile SEO tools and software

body_html:
A mobile SEO platform is any tool, or set of tools, that shows how your site performs for people and search engines on phones: how Google crawls the mobile version, how fast pages load and respond, and where you rank in mobile results. The right one depends on your site's size and how you report.

There's no single product that does everything. Most teams combine free Google tools with one or two paid tools. This post explains what to look for so you can compare options on features that matter instead of on marketing pages.

Why does mobile SEO need its own tools?

Google indexes and ranks the mobile version of your pages. Its documentation on mobile-first indexing best practices says Google uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with its smartphone crawler, for indexing and ranking. If something is missing or broken on mobile, Google may not see it, even if the desktop page looks fine.

So the questions you need answered are mobile-specific: does the mobile page have the same main content, headings, structured data and meta tags as desktop? How fast does it load and respond on real phones? Where do you rank when someone searches from a phone, often from a specific location?

Watch out Google retired its Mobile-Friendly Test and Search Console's Mobile Usability report in December 2023, as announced on the Search Central blog, and pointed people to Lighthouse instead. If a vendor or checklist still sends you there, or still reports First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital, it's out of date. That's a quick way to judge how current a tool is.

What should a mobile SEO platform do?

Use this table as your comparison checklist. The last column is what I'd actually do during a free trial, on your own site, before paying for anything.

FeatureWhy it mattersHow to test it in a trial
Crawls as a smartphoneGoogle indexes the mobile version, so the crawler should fetch pages with a smartphone user agent (the label a bot uses to say what device it is) and render JavaScriptCrawl a page whose content loads with scripts and confirm that content and its links show up
Compares mobile and desktopDynamic serving or a separate mobile site can drop text, titles, structured data or robots tags on phonesCrawl both versions of a few key templates and check that the tool flags differences
Real-user Core Web VitalsField data from real visitors is what Search Console reports; lab tests only simulate a visitCheck that it shows LCP, INP and CLS, labels field vs lab data, and splits mobile from desktop
Mobile rank tracking by locationMobile and desktop results can differ, and local results change from one area to the nextSet one keyword to mobile in your town and confirm you can pick both device and location
Search Console and GA4 connectionsSearch Console is Google's own data on clicks, impressions and indexing; GA4 shows what visitors do after they landConnect both and confirm the numbers match what you see in Google's own interfaces
Prioritized issuesLong warning lists don't help on their ownLook for grouping by template, a count of affected pages, and a way to mark issues fixed
Fits your size and teamA ten-page local site and a large store need different limitsCheck crawl limits, tracked keywords, user seats and scheduled crawls against your real numbers

The Core Web Vitals numbers a tool should report

Core Web Vitals are Google's three page experience measurements. INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. Google's Core Web Vitals report in Search Console uses real-user data, reports mobile and desktop separately, and lists these thresholds for "good":

2.5 sLargest Contentful Paint, loading (Search Console Help)

200 msInteraction to Next Paint, responsiveness (Search Console Help)

0.1Cumulative Layout Shift, visual stability (Search Console Help)

If a tool's "pass" doesn't line up with those numbers, ask the vendor what it's measuring. If you'd rather not manage rank tracking yourself, see my keyword tracking service.

Which tools make up a typical mobile SEO platform?

Tool typeExamplesWhat it answers
Google's free toolsSearch Console, PageSpeed Insights, Lighthouse in Chrome DevToolsHow Google sees your pages, real-user Core Web Vitals, lab performance audits
Site crawlersScreaming Frog, SitebulbTechnical issues across every page, mobile rendering, structured data
SEO suitesSemrush, AhrefsMobile rankings, competitors, site audits, keyword research
ReportingData Studio (formerly Looker Studio), GA4Combined dashboards and what visitors do after they land

These are examples, not endorsements. Feature sets change often, so confirm current capabilities in each tool's documentation or a free trial before you commit.

How do you choose the right mobile SEO platform?

Free Google tools are enough when

  • Your site has a few dozen pages and one main template
  • The site is fully responsive, with no separate mobile version
  • Search Console shows no Core Web Vitals or indexing problems
  • You serve one area and can check rankings by hand

Add a crawler or rank tracker when

  • You have more pages or templates than you can check by hand
  • Content is loaded by JavaScript or differs on phones
  • Search Console flags issues and you need to find which pages cause them
  • You report mobile rankings across several towns or clients

Score your own situation below. It weighs the same signals, so the result tells you which side you're closer to.

  • Your site has more than about 100 pages, or several page templates?
  • Search Console shows mobile URLs as "Poor" or "Need improvement" in the Core Web Vitals report?
  • Some content or links only appear after JavaScript runs, or your mobile site differs from desktop?
  • You need mobile rankings for more than one town or service area?
  • Someone other than you needs a regular report on mobile performance?

A crawler, a rank tracker or both will likely save you time. Shortlist two and test them on your own site.

Start with Search Console and PageSpeed Insights, and add one paid tool for the specific gap you scored on.

Google's free tools probably cover you for now. Check Search Console monthly and revisit this when the site grows.

Whichever way you go, plan who will act on the findings. A tool finds problems; someone still has to fix templates, images and scripts.

If you'd rather have someone audit your mobile setup and fix what matters most, see how my mobile SEO services work. For deeper crawl and indexing problems, my technical SEO services pick up where tools leave off.

Is Google Search Console enough for mobile SEO?

For small sites, it covers a lot: indexing, real-user Core Web Vitals, and search performance you can filter by device. What it doesn't do is crawl every page on demand, compare mobile and desktop versions side by side, or track rankings by location. Most growing sites add a crawler and a rank tracker once Search Console points to problems worth investigating.

Do you still need to test mobile usability now that Google's test is gone?

Yes. The tool was retired, not the need. Use Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools for lab checks, test key pages on real phones, and watch Search Console's Core Web Vitals report for real-user data. Pay attention to tap targets, text size, pop-ups that cover content, and forms that are hard to complete on a small screen.

How often should you run mobile SEO checks?

Check Search Console weekly or monthly, depending on how often your site changes. Run a full crawl after any redesign, migration, theme update, or new plugin, since those are common times for mobile issues to appear. Core Web Vitals data in Search Console is based on real visits over time, so give changes a few weeks before judging results.
